The House of Stuart. Ruling Scotland from 1371 and inheriting the English and Irish thrones in 1603, the Stuarts reigned until 1714. They navigated the treacherous waters of religious upheaval, civil war, and constitutional revolution, but their conflicts with Parliament over divine right and religious authority left deep scars on British political culture and eventually cost them their thrones.

James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, uniting the two kingdoms under one monarch. He believed in the divine right of kings, a doctrine that generated fierce conflict with an increasingly assertive Parliament. His son, Charles I, reigned from 1625 to 1649 and provoked the English Civil War through his religious policies and tyrannical rule. He was captured, tried for treason, and executed in 1649.

The Interregnum lasted from 1649 to 1660 under Oliver Cromwell's Commonwealth, during which the Stuart line was exiled. But Charles II was restored to the throne in 1660. His brother, James II, reigned from 1685 to 1688 as a Catholic convert. He sparked the Glorious Revolution in 1688 when his Protestant daughter Mary II and her husband William III of Orange took the throne instead. The Bill of Rights in 1689 established parliamentary supremacy over the monarchy, transforming British government forever.

The Stuart line ended with Queen Anne, who reigned from 1702 to 1714. The House of Hanover inherited Britain's thrones.
